overview: Visigothic royal power had an earlier centre at Toulouse and a later Iberian kingdom associated with Toledo. This card concentrates on the later kingdom, where excavated workshops and houses complement royal gifts, law and Latin scholarship. These different records show inventive adaptation of inherited traditions, but also inequalities and coercion within society.

periods.title: Toulouse as a royal centre
periods.summary: Visigoths settled at Toulouse in the early fifth century. The city served as a capital until 507; its royal buildings belong to an earlier phase than the Iberian examples below.

periods.title: A new royal city
periods.summary: Liuvigild's foundation of Reccopolis in 578 joined royal administration, worship, housing and manufacture within a planned city. Its workshops and water supply show substantial investment in urban life.

periods.title: Catholic monarchy and church institutions
periods.summary: Reccared's adoption of Catholic Christianity was proclaimed at the Third Council of Toledo in 589. Bishops and royal authority became closely connected, shaping government and religious expectations.

periods.title: Conquest and continuing settlements
periods.summary: Arab and Berber armies serving the Umayyad caliphate began conquering the kingdom in 711. Political authority changed through campaigns and agreements, while communities and some urban centres continued under new rulers.

sections.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis

items.text: Large houses in the early Visigothic city had circulation spaces leading to rooms, cooking areas and stables. Some were divided and enclosed during the seventh century. Changing walls and multiplying kitchens reveal households adapting existing buildings, rather than a town frozen in its founding plan.

Beside Reccopolis's main street, shops opened toward customers while workshops, stores and living spaces extended behind them. A circular glass furnace and associated processing structures survive. These remains place skilled production inside the town, close to both commercial activity and the palace approach.

The eastern craft building contained moulds for earrings and rings, balance pans and metalworking waste. Together these objects identify making and weighing, not merely possession of finished jewellery. They show the tools and discarded material behind the ornaments that survive in museum collections.

Reccopolis received water through a masonry aqueduct with a channel lined in waterproof mortar containing crushed ceramic. Surveyed remains preserve Roman construction principles in a late sixth-century project. Parts of its route remain missing and are reconstructed through terrain analysis rather than direct excavation.

Researchers argue that the aqueduct supplied more than the royal complex, proposing public distribution within the town. The volume of water and the hilltop setting support this interpretation. A complete network of household pipes and public fountains has not been excavated.

A tiled drain carried water from the courtyard of house 16000 toward the street. Other small drains and concave street surfaces suggest open channels for rain and overflow. This evidence should not be enlarged into a claim that the city possessed a complete underground sewer network.

The Guarrazar treasure includes gold crowns and crosses decorated with stones, pearls and cut crystal. Letters hanging from Recceswinth's crown identify its royal donor. These were offerings for religious settings; the suspended crown should not be imagined as the king's everyday headwear.

Guarrazar goldsmiths combined pierced or embossed sheets with settings and chains; some smaller crowns used open latticework. The treasure was concealed and later dispersed after its nineteenth-century discovery. Concealment shows an effort to protect valuable objects, but does not by itself establish one precise historical emergency.

Isidore of Seville's Etymologies organised subjects from grammar and mathematics to farming, textiles and household equipment through explanations of words. This was a work of compilation and interpretation. Its account of a craft does not establish that Isidore invented it or personally observed every process.

A manuscript of the Etymologies held by the Real Academia Espanola dates to the twelfth century, centuries after Isidore wrote. Such copies demonstrate the work's continuing transmission. The age of a surviving manuscript must be kept separate from the age of the text it carries.

A declaration addressed to Recceswinth in 654 required Jewish converts at Toledo to renounce Sabbath observance, religious festivals and dietary distinctions. Its coercive setting matters: the document records demands on a community, not free evidence that its members welcomed those demands.

Erwig's law of 681 threatened Jews who delayed baptism for themselves, their families or enslaved people with physical punishment, exile and confiscation. Royal religious uniformity came at others' expense. A prescribed penalty shows what authorities demanded, not proof that enforcement was identical everywhere.

ending.text: The Umayyad conquest began in 711 and displaced Visigothic royal government over several years. It did not remove the peninsula's whole population or immediately empty its towns. Reccopolis continued into the Islamic period before declining much later, and Isidore's work continued to be copied. The map endpoint of 800 is not the kingdom's fall date.
